Chapter 7—The Freedom of Letting Go: Releasing Control Over Others.
Have you ever noticed just how exhausting it is to try and manage everyone around you? Parents worrying over every move their kids make, partners trying to nudge each other’s habits, friends offering advice that’s really just a gentle push to change.
It almost always starts from a place of love, or care, or concern. But, more often than not, it ends up leaving everyone frustrated, distant, maybe even a little disappointed.
Picture a parent who only wants the best for their child. Every choice is weighed, every possible risk is managed, every misstep is quickly corrected. But here’s what usually happens—the child starts feeling that pressure and begins to pull away. The parent, picking up on that distance, tries even harder to guide and protect. And suddenly, you’ve got a cycle where both sides feel misunderstood and stuck.
This pattern? It’s more common than you might think. And at the heart of it is a simple misunderstanding: the idea that you can create happiness for someone else, or guarantee their safety, or that loving someone means controlling their choices.
But here’s the truth—each of us has to live our own life. No matter how much you worry, or how hard you try, you can’t make someone else choose happiness, or keep them from pain, or force them to grow in the way you want.
Letting go of control doesn’t mean giving up on someone. It’s actually an act of trust. It’s believing that the people you care about are capable, that they deserve to make their own choices—even if that means making mistakes. It’s about being there for them, not steering them.
Think about a friend facing a tough decision. The urge to jump in, to offer the perfect solution, to guide them down the “right” path—it’s strong, isn’t it? But what if, instead, you just listened? What if you asked questions, and trusted that your friend would find their own way? Suddenly, the whole conversation changes. Your friend feels heard, not managed. And the relationship gets stronger.
This kind of freedom—letting go of control—is rare. It doesn’t always come naturally, especially when most of us have been taught that caring means fixing, that love means guiding. But real connection? That comes from respect, from letting others be themselves, letting them grow in their own time, and in their own way.
In families, it might look like giving a teenager space to stumble and learn, even when it’s tough to watch. In a partnership, it means accepting your differences, letting go of the urge to change each other. And with friends, it’s about offering support without expecting anything in return—advice without strings attached.
When you do this, something amazing happens. You start to feel lighter. You’re no longer carrying the weight of responsibility for everyone else’s happiness. Relationships shift; they become more about companionship than control.
And honestly, the courage to let go is also the courage to be disliked sometimes—to trust others with their own lives, and to trust yourself with your own.
Over time, that freedom grows. The urge to direct or fix fades away. In its place, you’ll discover a quiet confidence, a sense of peace. The world may not be perfect, and neither are the people in it. But everyone is free to walk their own path, and find their own way.
